references.text: The main text in the Old Testament that Luke 17:29 directly refers to: The Lord rained down sulfur and fire from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah and destroyed the cities. [ref:Gen 19:24-25|Genesis 19:24-25] is the historical account of Lot's departure from Sodom and the subsequent destruction.

Lot was led out of Sodom by angels before the destruction came. [ref:Gen 19:16-17|Genesis 19:16-17] describes the actual departure from the city that Luke refers to with the words "the day Lot left Sodom".
[ref:Deut 29:23|Deuteronomy 29:23] uses the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah by sulfur and fire as a warning example of God's judgment, just as Jesus does in Luke 17.
[ref:Isa 13:19|Isaiah 13:19] compares Babylon's coming destruction with God's destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, showing how this event became a pattern for God's final judgment.
[ref:Jer 50:40|Jeremiah 50:40] refers to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah as an image of total and irreversible judgment, just as Jesus uses it in his speech about the day of the Son of Man.

[ref:Luk 17:26-28|Luke 17:26-28] gives the immediate context: Jesus compares the day of the Son of Man with the days of Noah and Lot – people lived their daily lives until judgment suddenly came, just as fire and sulfur rained down on Sodom.

[ref:Luk 17:30|Luke 17:30] applies the Sodom example directly: "So it will be also on the day when the Son of Man is revealed." The destruction of Sodom is a pattern for the sudden judgment at Jesus' return.

[ref:2 Pet 2:6-7|2 Peter 2:6-7] mentions that God reduced Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and condemned them to destruction as an example for the ungodly, but saved the righteous Lot – the same pattern Jesus highlights in Luke 17:29.

[ref:Jude 1:7|Jude 1:7] refers to Sodom and Gomorrah as examples of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire, confirming the typological use of the fire judgment over Sodom as an image of God's final judgment.

[ref:Rev 14:10|Revelation 14:10] uses the images of fire and sulfur to describe the eschatological judgment, linking back to the original fire-and-sulfur judgment over Sodom that Jesus refers to in Luke 17:29.
